docs.title: infrapi/lib
docs.text:
Opinionated Go building blocks shared by InfraPI services. Eight small packages, no framework:

Package Import path What it does cluster github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/cluster Runs a service as coordinated replicas: a ring per role, leader or broadcast. Its own module. config github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/config Reads a dotenv file, validates values, exposes a typed AppConfig. errors github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/errors RFC 9457 application error with an HTTP status, a cause and a remediation hint. gateway github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/gateway Typed CRUD client for the Apache APISIX Admin API: routes, services, upstreams, consumers. http github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/http Resty-based API client with TLS/mTLS, retry and hedging. listener github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/listener Opens the service socket, TCP or systemd socket activation. server github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/server gin.Engine pre-wired with CORS, trusted proxies, Prometheus metrics and generated OpenAPI docs. tofu github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/tofu Drives any OpenTofu provider plugin and resource type, and applies a declarative set of providers and resources on top.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
go get github.com/infrapi/lib

cluster is a module of its own, so that a service which does not cluster does not inherit the dependency tree of dskit:

go get github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/cluster

Requires Go 1.26.7 or later.

docs.title: In one minute
docs.text:
package main

import (
    "log"

    "github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/config"
    "github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/server"
)

func main() {
    vars, err := config.NewConfig()
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    cfg, err := vars.GetAppConfig()
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    engine, err := server.NewServerGin(cfg)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }

    if err := engine.Run(cfg.AppListenAddress); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

Continue with Getting started.

make all

runs setup clean tidy fmt lint security test. The individual targets:

Target Command setup installs golangci-lint, gosec and goreleaser if missing tidy go mod tidy fmt gofmt -w on every tracked Go file lint golangci-lint run security gosec -exclude-dir _local -quiet ./... test go test with coverage, writes cover.out and coverage.html

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The site is MkDocs Material. Install the toolchain once:

pip install mkdocs mkdocs-material pymdown-extensions mkdocs-git-revision-date-localized-plugin

Then:

make docs         # build into site/
make docs-serve   # live reload on http://localhost:8000
make docs-deploy  # push to the gh-pages branch

Pages live in docs/ and the navigation is declared in mkdocs.yml. A new page must be added to nav:, otherwise the CI build - which runs mkdocs build --strict - fails.

Pushing to the default branch publishes the site through GitHub Pages; make docs-deploy is only needed for a manual out-of-band publish.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
pkg/config    dotenv loading, validation, AppConfig
pkg/errors    RFC 9457 error carried back to API clients
pkg/http      resty-based API client
pkg/listener  service socket, TCP or systemd socket activation
pkg/server    gin engine factory, metrics and OpenAPI endpoints
examples/     one runnable program per package
docs/         this site

Tests sit next to the code they cover and use real HTTP servers and real dotenv files rather than mocks. New code is expected to arrive with tests in the same style.

docs.title: 1. Add the dependency
docs.text: go get github.com/infrapi/lib

docs.title: 2. Write a dotenv file
docs.text:
Configuration comes from a dotenv file, not from the process environment. The only environment variable the library reads directly is INFRAPI_CONFIG_DOTENV_FILE, which points at that file (default: .env in the working directory).

.env
INFRAPI_APP_NAME="my-service"
INFRAPI_APP_PLATFORM="sandbox"
INFRAPI_APP_REGION="eu-west-1"
INFRAPI_APP_LOCATION="dc1"
INFRAPI_APP_URL="http://my-service.example.com:8080"
INFRAPI_APP_LISTEN_ADDRESS="127.0.0.1:8080"

INFRAPI_APP_NAME, INFRAPI_APP_PLATFORM, INFRAPI_APP_REGION, INFRAPI_APP_LOCATION and INFRAPI_APP_URL have no default value, so GetAppConfig() fails without them. Everything else falls back to the defaults listed in the config reference.

docs.title: 3. Load the configuration
docs.text:
vars, err := config.NewConfig()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err) // dotenv file missing or unreadable
}

cfg, err := vars.GetAppConfig()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err) // a key is missing or fails its validator
}

docs.title: 4. Serve
docs.text:
engine, err := server.NewServerGin(cfg)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

engine.GET("/api/v1/widgets", func(c *gin.Context) {
    c.JSON(http.StatusOK, gin.H{"widgets": []string{"foo", "bar"}})
})

if err := engine.Run(cfg.AppListenAddress); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

The engine already answers GET /-/metadata with the application identity.

docs.title: 5. Call another service
docs.text:
client, err := infrahttp.NewClient(&infrahttp.ClientOptions{
    Server:      "api.example.com",
    Application: "myapp",
    Token:       os.Getenv("INFRAPI_TOKEN"),
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

resp, err := client.Get("status", nil)

That request hits https://api.example.com:443/api/v1/myapp/status. See the http reference for TLS, retry and hedging options.

docs.title: Runnable examples
docs.text:
Each package has a self-contained program under examples/:

go run ./examples/config
go run ./examples/errors
go run ./examples/http
go run ./examples/listener
go run ./examples/server

examples/config, examples/listener and examples/server expect to be run from the repository root: they point INFRAPI_CONFIG_DOTENV_FILE at dotenv files shipped next to the source.

The cluster examples are the exception twice over. They are a Go module of their own, so that importing cluster does not pull dskit into the root module, and there is one directory per use case rather than one program:

cd examples/cluster/leader && go run .

examples/cluster/README.md lists them all. examples/cluster/node is the one worth running twice, in two terminals, for a real two-node cluster.

docs.title: cluster
docs.text:
import "github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/cluster"

Runs a service as several coordinated replicas, on top of dskit: a key-value store every replica shares, one hash ring per role, and a lifecycler that registers this replica and keeps its heartbeat fresh.

What a service actually gets out of it is one predicate.

should, err := role.ShouldRun()

Its own Go module

cluster is a separate module, so a service that does not cluster does not inherit dskit's dependency tree — grpc, etcd, consul, otel, hashicorp/memberlist.

go get github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/cluster

The cost of that split: because Role.Ring, Role.Lifecycler and Cluster.KVClient return dskit types, this package's API is pinned to one dskit pseudo-version. A breaking change there is a breaking change here.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
A role is one ring. A service declares its roles in Go, because the coordination mode decides what the application code does; the dotenv lists which of them this replica joins, the way Mimir's -target does.

appConfig, _ := vars.GetAppConfig()
clusterConfig, _ := vars.GetClusterConfig()

c, err := cluster.New(appConfig, clusterConfig, cluster.Options{
    Roles: []cluster.RoleSpec{
        {Name: "scheduler", Mode: cluster.ModeLeader},
        {Name: "collector", Mode: cluster.ModeBroadcast},
    },
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}

if err := c.Start(ctx); err != nil {
    return err
}
defer func() { _ = c.Stop(context.Background()) }()

INFRAPI_CLUSTER_ROLES=["scheduler","collector"]
Mismatch What happens A name in the dotenv the code does not declare New fails with ErrRoleUndeclared. It is always a typo or a bad rollout, and a silent no-op would mean a scheduler that never schedules with nothing in the logs. A declared role the dotenv does not select Accepted. A binary legitimately knows more roles than a deployment runs; Cluster.Role reports ErrRoleNotJoined. Roles declared, none selected New fails with ErrNoRoles. A cluster that joins no ring coordinates nothing. No roles declared at all Accepted: a store with no rings, for a service that wants shared state and no coordination.

Two roles that share a name, or a ring key, are refused by New. They would both register the same Prometheus collectors, and promauto panics rather than returning an error.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
const (
    cluster.ModeLeader    // only the owner of the leader token acts
    cluster.ModeBroadcast // every healthy member acts
)
ModeLeader ModeBroadcast ShouldRun is true on the owner of the leader token every healthy member Ring states accepted ACTIVE, LEAVING ACTIVE Leader, IsLeader the elected replica ErrWrongMode

ModeLeader counts a LEAVING replica as eligible, which is what keeps a rolling restart from changing leader at every step. ModeBroadcast does not: a replica that is draining must stop working.

A non-nil error from ShouldRun means do not act. It says the ring view is unusable, not that this replica was excluded.

docs.title: A gated periodic action
docs.text:
err := role.Run(ctx, 30*time.Second, func(runCtx context.Context) error {
    return reconcile(runCtx)
})

Run re-checks ShouldRun on every tick, never overlaps two runs, and cancels the action's context as soon as this replica stops being eligible. An error from the action is logged and the loop continues: a transient empty ring during a gossip partition must not kill a service's control loop.

The ring is not a distributed lock

Leader election here is ownership of a ring token, refreshed by heartbeat. There is no quorum and no lease. During a network partition two replicas can each believe they are the leader, and the cancellation Run performs is cooperative: an action that ignores its context, or is blocked in a syscall, keeps running.

The overlap is bounded by INFRAPI_CLUSTER_HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT plus one watchdog interval. Nothing closes it. The action must be idempotent, or fenced by whatever it writes to — a compare-and-swap, a conditional write, a unique constraint.

docs.title: Two separations not to confuse
docs.text:
This is the part that costs an afternoon if it is got wrong.

Set by Decides Gossip cluster label INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_CLUSTER_LABEL Which gossip mesh a replica belongs to. memberlist discards any packet whose label does not match, so a wrong label makes a replica invisible rather than noisy. Ring key INFRAPI_CLUSTER_KV_PREFIX + the role name Which ring inside that mesh.

Replicas sharing a label gossip with each other and ignore each other's rings. That is what lets several different services join one mesh and each register in the ring of its own role, which is how Mimir runs an ingester ring, a ruler ring and a compactor ring over one cluster.

gossip mesh, label "prod-eu-west-1"
  collectors/scheduler  -> the ring of role "scheduler" (leader)
  collectors/collector  -> the ring of role "collector" (broadcast)
  collectors/state      -> whatever a caller codec writes

Changing the label on a live cluster needs two rollouts, with INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_CLUSTER_LABEL_VERIFICATION_DISABLED=true in between.

RoleSpec.Key overrides the key, and exists for one reason: adopting this package on a deployment whose ring is already written under a different key, without resetting it.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
INFRAPI_CLUSTER_KV_STORE selects the store. Everything above it is backend-agnostic.

Store Use memberlist Gossip between replicas. No external dependency, one TCP port. The default. etcd A central store, when one is already operated. inmemory A process-wide map. Tests and single-replica runs only: it coordinates nothing beyond the process, so two replicas on it each get their own ring and each elect themselves. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_JOIN_MEMBERS with it is refused, which is the one mistake it can catch for you.

dskit also implements a consul store and a mirroring multi store for migrating between two backends. Neither is wired up here; both would cost one widened validator and a key block.

The gossip store is memory, and only memory

There is no persistence in it at all — no snapshot, no file, nothing on disk. The cluster's own memory is the storage, replicated across whichever replicas happen to be alive.

A replica that restarts recovers by pulling the state from a live peer, so a rolling restart is safe. Stopping every replica at once loses everything: a bad rollout that restarts them together, a region-wide outage, a scale to zero. Nothing warns you, and nothing brings it back.

So the gossip store holds coordination state that can be rebuilt — who is a member, who leads, a view derived from somewhere else. It is not a system of record. If the data has to survive the cluster, either use etcd, which persists it, or treat the gossip store as a cache each replica repopulates at startup from the real source of truth.

Store Survives a full cluster stop? memberlist No. Memory only, replicated across live replicas. etcd Yes, to etcd's disk. inmemory No, and not even a process restart.

The gossip transport is TCP only

dskit's memberlist transport uses TCP for both its packet and its stream traffic. One port, no UDP: a firewall rule needs TCP 7946 and nothing else.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Every key is read from the dotenv through config.GetClusterConfig, which stops on the first key that is missing or fails its validator, then checks the rules that span several keys.

docs.title: Core
docs.text: Key Default Notes INFRAPI_CLUSTER_ENABLED false Off means New still returns a usable object whose Start is a no-op and whose queries report ErrDisabled. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_KV_STORE memberlist memberlist, etcd or inmemory. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_KV_PREFIX collectors/ Must end in /. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_ROLES [] The roles this replica joins. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_INSTANCE_ID the host name The ring identity, and the gossip node name. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_INSTANCE_ADDR auto-detected Optional; otherwise found from the interface names below. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_INSTANCE_INTERFACE_NAMES ["eth0", "en0"] INFRAPI_CLUSTER_INSTANCE_PORT 7946 The port advertised in the ring. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_START_TIMEOUT 30s Bounds the whole of Start. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_STOP_TIMEOUT 45s Must exceed the gossip leave timeout plus the broadcast drain. A ceiling, not a wait.

docs.title: Ring and lifecycler
docs.text: Key Default Notes INFRAPI_CLUSTER_HEARTBEAT_PERIOD 15s INFRAPI_CLUSTER_HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT 1m Must be greater than the period, or every replica flaps. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_KEEP_INSTANCE_IN_RING_ON_SHUTDOWN true See the failover note below. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_AUTO_FORGET_UNHEALTHY_PERIODS 10 Multiples of the heartbeat timeout. 0 disables it; 1 is refused. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_TOKENS_OBSERVE_PERIOD 0s

docs.title: Zones
docs.text:
Key Default Notes INFRAPI_CLUSTER_ZONE INFRAPI_APP_LOCATION Where this replica runs. At most 16 bytes: it travels in every gossip packet. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_ZONE_AWARENESS_ENABLED false Ring-level: spread a key's replicas across zones. Does nothing until a role's replication factor is above 1. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_EXCLUDED_ZONES [] Zones to filter out of this replica's view of the ring. Listing your own is refused. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_ZONE_AWARE_ROUTING_ENABLED false Gossip-level: keep gossip inside a zone. Read the next section before enabling it. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_ZONE_ROLE member member gossips only within its zone; bridge also reaches bridges in other zones.

There is no key for the replication factor or the token count. Both are semantics of the coordination mode, which lives in code: an operator who could set a replication factor of 3 on a leader ring would break the election, so the dotenv must not be able to express it. RoleSpec.NumTokens is the override, in the same place as the decision it belongs to.

docs.title: Gossip
docs.text:
Applies only when the store is memberlist.

Key Default INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_CLUSTER_LABEL infrapi INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_CLUSTER_LABEL_VERIFICATION_DISABLED false INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_BIND_ADDRS ["0.0.0.0"] INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_BIND_PORT 7946 (0 for an ephemeral port) INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_ADVERTISE_ADDR unset (NAT traversal) INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_ADVERTISE_PORT 0 INFRAPI_CLUSTER_JOIN_MEMBERS [] INFRAPI_CLUSTER_JOIN_MIN_BACKOFF 1s INFRAPI_CLUSTER_JOIN_MAX_BACKOFF 1m INFRAPI_CLUSTER_JOIN_MAX_RETRIES 10 INFRAPI_CLUSTER_ABORT_IF_JOIN_FAILS false INFRAPI_CLUSTER_REJOIN_INTERVAL 0s INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_INTERVAL 200ms INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_NODES 3 INFRAPI_CLUSTER_PUSH_PULL_INTERVAL 30s INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_TO_THE_DEAD_TIME 30s INFRAPI_CLUSTER_LEAVE_TIMEOUT 20s INFRAPI_CLUSTER_BROADCAST_TIMEOUT_ON_SHUTDOWN 10s INFRAPI_CLUSTER_OBSOLETE_ENTRIES_TIMEOUT 30s (a fully deleted key) INFRAPI_CLUSTER_TOMBSTONE_TIMEOUT 5m (a deleted entry inside a value) INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_COMPRESSION_ENABLED true INFRAPI_CLUSTER_MESSAGE_HISTORY_BUFFER_BYTES 0 INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_TLS_ENABLED false INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_TLS_CA_PATH unset INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_TLS_CERT_PATH unset INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_TLS_KEY_PATH unset INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_TLS_SERVER_NAME unset INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_TLS_INSECURE_SKIP_VERIFY false

INFRAPI_CLUSTER_ABORT_IF_JOIN_FAILS=true is worth knowing about: without it, a replica that cannot reach its seed nodes starts anyway, forms a cluster of one, and elects itself. Two of those are indistinguishable from a working cluster until something goes wrong.

INFRAPI_CLUSTER_MESSAGE_HISTORY_BUFFER_BYTES is 0, and should stay there. It keeps every message the node sends and receives in memory, so it buys the message history on the gossip page at the cost of carrying that buffer for as long as the process lives. Turn it on while troubleshooting, turn it back off afterwards.

docs.text:
Applies only when the store is etcd.

docs.title: What is left at dskit's defaults
docs.text:
Stream timeouts, retransmit factor, dead node reclaim time, the message queue sizes, the compression algorithm, the CAS retry backoffs, the TCP transport's packet timeouts and write concurrency, the TLS cipher suites and minimum version, zone awareness, and the whole consul and multi-store surface.

The rule for adding a key: an operator would plausibly change it to fix a production problem, or a test needs it to run fast. Everything above is either a dskit internal tuning constant or a knob whose correct value is "whatever dskit says".

docs.title: Several data centres
docs.text:
Two unrelated dskit features are both called zone awareness, and choosing the wrong one is how a multi-DC cluster ends up split without anyone noticing.

Key What it decides Ring INFRAPI_CLUSTER_ZONE_AWARENESS_ENABLED How many replicas share a piece of work, and where. With a replication factor above 1, the ring puts those replicas in different zones. Gossip INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_ZONE_AWARE_ROUTING_ENABLED Who talks to whom. Whether a replica gossips with every peer or only with those in its own zone.

The replication factor is the first of those, and it is not what decides whether replicas in different data centres talk to each other. The two modes shipped here both use a single replica, so ring zone awareness has nothing to spread until a role raises RoleSpec.ReplicationFactor.

What follows is the second one: three topologies, and they are genuinely different deployments rather than three settings of the same one.

docs.title: Everyone talks to everyone
docs.text:
The default. One mesh, every replica gossiping with every other, whatever data centre it sits in. One ring per role, spanning all of them, so a role elects one leader across the whole deployment.

INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_CLUSTER_LABEL="prod"
# zone-aware routing left off

Simple, and the right answer until cross-DC gossip traffic becomes a problem. Every replica holds the whole state and chatters with everyone.

docs.title: One mesh, gossip kept local, bridges between zones
docs.text:
Still one logical cluster and one ring per role, but gossip stays inside a zone instead of crossing between every pair of replicas. A handful of replicas are promoted to bridge and carry traffic between zones.

# every replica
INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_CLUSTER_LABEL="prod"
INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_ZONE_AWARE_ROUTING_ENABLED="true"
INFRAPI_CLUSTER_ZONE="dc1"           # or dc2, dc3

# most of them
INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_ZONE_ROLE="member"

# at least one per zone
INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_ZONE_ROLE="bridge"

A member selects only peers in its own zone. A bridge selects its own zone, plus the bridges of other zones. So the bridges are the only path state takes between data centres.

A zone without a live bridge degrades, it does not split

dskit notices. When a zone has no bridge alive, it abandons zone-aware routing and goes back to selecting every peer, logging memberlist zone-aware routing is skipped because a zone has no alive bridge and counting it in infrapi_cluster_memberlist_client_zone_aware_routing_select_nodes_skipped_total.

So losing a zone's bridges costs the traffic saving, not the cluster: the ring stays whole and keeps one leader. Verified by running examples/cluster/zones and killing a bridge — the remaining three replicas still agree on their membership and their leader.

Run at least two bridges per zone anyway, and alert on that counter: a cluster silently gossiping full-mesh is doing the thing you turned this on to avoid.

docs.title: Independent clusters, one per data centre
docs.text:
If replicas genuinely should not coordinate across data centres — a leader per DC rather than one leader overall — then do not reach for zone-aware routing at all. Give each DC its own gossip cluster label:

# dc1
INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_CLUSTER_LABEL="prod-dc1"
# dc2
INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_CLUSTER_LABEL="prod-dc2"

memberlist discards any packet whose label does not match, so these are separate meshes with separate rings, by construction and not by configuration that could drift. No bridges, no split-brain risk, no cross-DC traffic. It is the right answer whenever the work itself is per-DC.

Choosing between the last two comes down to one question: is there one leader for the whole deployment, or one per data centre? One overall needs a single mesh and bridges; one per DC needs separate labels. Note that the middle option is a traffic optimisation, not an isolation mechanism: every replica still ends up holding the whole cluster's state. If zones must not know about each other, only separate labels give you that.

examples/cluster/zones runs this topology on one machine — two zones, a bridge and a member in each — and its README walks through killing a bridge.

docs.title: Affinity: work handled in its own data centre
docs.text:
Zone-aware routing does not give you this. It decides who gossips with whom, not who acts: the ring spans every zone and elects one leader wherever the token lands, which may well be the other side of the country. Two ways to get affinity instead, and they differ in whether the data centres can still see each other.

One ring per data centre, one mesh. A role is a ring, so a role named after the zone gives each data centre its own leader election while every replica stays in one cluster — and can therefore read every other zone's ring on the status pages.

zone := clusterConfig.Zone // or appConfig.AppLocation

c, err := cluster.New(appConfig, clusterConfig, cluster.Options{
    Roles: []cluster.RoleSpec{
        // Every zone the binary may run in, declared up front.
        {Name: "scheduler-dc1", Mode: cluster.ModeLeader},
        {Name: "scheduler-dc2", Mode: cluster.ModeLeader},

        // And one ring the whole deployment shares, if something does need a
        // single leader overall.
        {Name: "migrations", Mode: cluster.ModeLeader},
    },
})

# in dc1
INFRAPI_CLUSTER_ROLES=["scheduler-dc1","migrations"]
# in dc2
INFRAPI_CLUSTER_ROLES=["scheduler-dc2","migrations"]

Each scheduler-dcN ring holds only the replicas of that data centre and elects one of them; migrations spans all of them and elects one overall. A replica asking for a role it did not join gets ErrRoleNotJoined, so a misrouted deployment fails loudly rather than acting in the wrong place.

One cluster per data centre. If the zones should not see each other at all, give each its own INFRAPI_CLUSTER_GOSSIP_CLUSTER_LABEL, as above. Separate meshes, separate rings, nothing shared, no cross-DC traffic. Pick this when there is nothing a replica in one data centre would ever want to know about another.

What neither gives you is key-level affinity — "this particular job belongs to dc1". That needs a sharded mode, where a key maps to a ring token, and it is not implemented here.

docs.title: Keeping a zone out
docs.text: INFRAPI_CLUSTER_EXCLUDED_ZONES filters instances out of this replica's view of the ring, whatever the gossip layer does. It is a blunt instrument for draining a data centre: the replicas there stay in the mesh and keep gossiping, but this replica stops counting them as members or electing them leader. Listing your own zone is refused, since it would leave this replica reading an empty ring and never acting.

docs.title: Status pages
docs.text:
engine, err := server.NewServerGin(appConfig)
if err != nil {
    return err
}

if err := c.RegisterGin(engine, cluster.HandlerOptions{}); err != nil {
    return err
}
Path Serves GET /-/cluster This package's JSON summary: identity, store, label, and per role its mode, members, leader and whether this replica should act. GET /-/cluster/ring/{role} dskit's ring page. Honours Accept: application/json. GET /-/cluster/memberlist dskit's gossip page, or 404 when the store is not memberlist.

The paths come from HandlerOptions.PathPrefix, which defaults to DefaultPathPrefix.

They mount before Start and explain themselves until the cluster is up, so a service can wire its routes once at startup. A role that cannot be read reports its own error rather than failing the whole page: during a partition, which roles are readable is the useful part.

HandlerOptions.ForgetEnabled also mounts the ring page's POST route, which evicts a replica from the ring. That is an unauthenticated write to cluster state, so it is off unless a deployment asks for it.

HandlerOptions.PathPrefix relocates the whole set, for instance under /debug/cluster.

docs.title: The gossip page: dskit's data, this design
docs.text:
/-/cluster/memberlist shows what dskit's own page shows — the key-value store, the gossip membership, and the message history — because that introspection could not be reproduced from outside dskit anyway: the data behind it is unexported.

What is ours is the rendering. memberlist.NewHTTPStatusHandler takes a template, so the page is laid out in this package, in the same design as the others, instead of dskit's unstyled default. dskit's own actions survive with it: the ?viewKey=, ?viewMsg= and ?downloadKey= links still work, because the handler is still dskit's and only the template was replaced. Those responses are text and raw dumps rather than pages, and come back untouched.

Section What it tells you Health score memberlist's own view of this node. 0 is healthy; anything higher means it is struggling to reach peers. Cluster members Who is in the mesh, with its gossip state — alive, suspect, dead, left. Not the same thing as a ring: a node appears here as soon as it joined, whatever rings it registered in. Key-value store One row per key, with the codec, the node-local version, the encoded size, and links to inspect or download the value. Message history What this node sent and received. Empty unless INFRAPI_CLUSTER_MESSAGE_HISTORY_BUFFER_BYTES is set, which is off by default because it buffers every message in memory; the page names the key rather than rendering empty tables.

Role.LifecyclerHandler is the one page still rendered by dskit, so that one gets the stylesheet injected into its head rather than a template of its own.

docs.title: Mounting them where you already look
docs.text:
The /-/ prefix is this library's convention, and the ring page is per role because there are now several rings. Other dskit-based services — Mimir, and acme-manager — put a single ring at /ring and the gossip page at /memberlist, and runbooks and dashboards point there.

Both handlers take no path parameter, so that layout is four lines:

engine.GET("/memberlist", c.MemberlistHandler())

scheduler, err := c.Role("scheduler")
if err != nil {
    return err
}
engine.GET("/ring", scheduler.RingHandler())

Role.LifecyclerHandler renders the same page from this replica's lifecycler instead of from the ring service. The only difference is the source: the lifecycler reads the key-value store on every request, the ring serves the snapshot it already watches. Prefer RingHandler; LifecyclerHandler is there for a deployment that wants the uncached view, or that previously mounted the lifecycler and wants the same bytes.

The serve mode of the example mounts both layouts side by side, so the two can be compared on a live cluster.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Everything dskit registers is prefixed infrapi_cluster_ and goes on prometheus.DefaultRegisterer, which the server package already exposes at /-/metrics. Nothing else to wire.

infrapi_cluster_ring_members{name="scheduler",state="ACTIVE"}
infrapi_cluster_ring_member_heartbeats_total{name="scheduler"}
infrapi_cluster_kv_request_duration_seconds{kv_name="scheduler-ring"}
infrapi_cluster_memberlist_client_cluster_members_count

The prefix is not decoration: dskit names its collectors ring_members, kv_request_duration_seconds and dns_lookups_total, with no namespace of their own.

Only one cluster per registerer. dns_lookups_total carries no label that would tell two of them apart, so a second cluster on the same registerer is refused by New rather than left to panic — pass Options.Registerer if a process really needs two.

docs.title: Sharing application state
docs.text:
The store the rings use also carries application state. The codec must be declared up front: the gossip store only learns its codecs when the replica joins, and a client built later for an unregistered codec is refused.

stateCodec := codec.NewProtoCodec("fleet-state", func() proto.Message { return &FleetState{} })

c, err := cluster.New(appConfig, clusterConfig, cluster.Options{
    Roles:  roles,
    Codecs: []codec.Codec{stateCodec},
})
...
client, err := c.KVClient("fleet-state")

With the gossip store the value must also implement memberlist.Mergeable, and its Merge must be idempotent, commutative and associative — a CRDT. Gossip delivers updates out of order and more than once, and nothing reconciles afterwards, so a merge without those properties leaves replicas in different states permanently. A value that is not Mergeable fails loudly (invalid type: …, expected Mergeable), but a Mergeable whose merge is subtly wrong fails silently: test the three properties directly.

The etcd and in-memory clients impose no such thing — they encode, decode and compare-and-swap — so a bare protobuf message works there, and will not move to the gossip store later.

examples/cluster/state-proto carries a worked example: the proto, the hand-written type, and the property tests.

docs.title: Deleting: what actually happens, and when it is really gone
docs.text:
This is the part worth understanding before designing around it, because a deletion is real but it is not immediate, and three different settings govern three different stages.

Deleting is an update. Do not remove the entry — write it back with a deleted flag. Two reasons, and both are hard:

  • WatchPrefix does not report deletions. dskit skips its callback when the value comes back nil, which is exactly what a key whose value was deleted gives. (WatchKey does report them, with a nil value, but you can only watch a key you already know about.) An entry carrying a flag is never nil, so every watcher is told like any other change.
  • On gossip, a peer that never heard about the removal would re-add the entry at the next merge. The flag is what lets Merge decide that "deleted at T2" supersedes "present at T1".

Then it is gone in three stages, and only the last one frees anything:

Stage Governed by Default What it does Hidden from the application nothing — every read — The store calls RemoveTombstones with a zero limit before handing a value over, so a deleted entry never reaches your code. Still gossiped INFRAPI_CLUSTER_TOMBSTONE_TIMEOUT 5m The entry stays in the value and keeps propagating, so a replica that was down or partitioned still learns of the deletion when it comes back. After this it may be dropped for good. The whole key removed INFRAPI_CLUSTER_OBSOLETE_ENTRIES_TIMEOUT 30s Only applies to a key whose entire value was deleted, which is what kv.Client.Delete does. Not your per-entry flag.

The one to reason about is the middle row. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_TOMBSTONE_TIMEOUT is how long the cluster remembers that something was deleted — so it is also the longest a replica may be absent and still come back converged. A replica away for longer than that can rejoin holding an entry everyone else has forgotten, and re-introduce it. Set it longer than your worst realistic outage, not shorter: the cost is a little state and bandwidth, and the alternative is an item coming back from the dead.

dskit names that setting -memberlist.left-ingesters-timeout and documents it in ring terms, which is why it is easy to miss: it is the limit passed to RemoveTombstones on any gossiped value, not just on ring membership.

The store is a membership store, not a cache

Every key costs a broadcast worker and a slot in the state each replica gossips, on every push/pull. Keys must be few and long-lived.

A key per request, per job or per challenge is how this becomes an out-of-memory incident: the workers accumulate, and the state each replica carries grows without bound. If state is per-item and short-lived, it does not belong here.

docs.title: Shutdown, and the failover delay
docs.text:
Stop leaves every role ring and then the store, in reverse order. It ignores cancellation of its context on purpose: a shutdown is normally triggered because the caller's context was cancelled, and honouring it would abandon the gossip leave.

Budget it properly. The gossip leave costs the broadcast drain (INFRAPI_CLUSTER_BROADCAST_TIMEOUT_ON_SHUTDOWN, 10s) plus the leave itself (INFRAPI_CLUSTER_LEAVE_TIMEOUT, 20s), and each role's lifecycler takes its turn before any of that. INFRAPI_CLUSTER_STOP_TIMEOUT below the sum of the first two is refused at load time, because it would guarantee a truncated leave: this replica would then be remembered as dead rather than gone, and every peer would keep it in the ring until its heartbeat went stale. The budget is a ceiling, so a shutdown with nothing left to say still returns at once.

A dying leader keeps its token

With INFRAPI_CLUSTER_KEEP_INSTANCE_IN_RING_ON_SHUTDOWN=true, the default, a stopping replica sits in LEAVING — which a leader role counts as eligible. A dying leader therefore keeps the leader token until its heartbeat goes stale, up to INFRAPI_CLUSTER_HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT.

That is the trade: far fewer leader changes across a rolling restart, at the price of up to a minute of nothing running at the defaults. Shorten the heartbeat timeout, or set the key to false to make planned failover immediate at the cost of a leader change on every restart.

A cluster is single use: dskit services cannot be restarted. A Start that fails means the process should exit, not rebuild the Cluster — the collectors of the failed attempt are already registered. Err delivers the first asynchronous failure of any underlying service, and a value on it means the same thing.

docs.title: Running the examples
docs.text:
examples/cluster holds one directory per use case, each runnable on its own:

cd examples/cluster/leader     && go run .   # leader mode
cd examples/cluster/broadcast  && go run .   # broadcast mode
cd examples/cluster/roles      && go run .   # several roles, a ring each
cd examples/cluster/gated      && go run .   # Role.Run
cd examples/cluster/state      && go run .   # sharing state through the store
cd examples/cluster/pages      && go run .   # these status pages
cd examples/cluster/shutdown   && go run .   # Stop, and what queries say after

Each carries its own app.env, so one directory tells you exactly which keys that case needs. They are a Go module of their own, so they run from their own directory rather than with go run ./examples/....

All seven use the in-memory store: no socket, no peer, done in under a second. They show the API. The one that shows the behaviour is node/.

docs.title: Two real replicas
docs.text:
Clustering is the one thing here that cannot be shown in one process. Two terminals, from examples/cluster/node:

INFRAPI_CONFIG_DOTENV_FILE=node1.env go run .
INFRAPI_CONFIG_DOTENV_FILE=node2.env go run .

node2.env differs from node1.env only in its identity, its two ports, and the seed node it joins. Each replica prints what it believes once a second:

node-1 | scheduler(leader): members=2 leader=node-1 -> ACTING  | collector(broadcast): members=2 -> ACTING
node-2 | scheduler(leader): members=2 leader=node-1 -> passive | collector(broadcast): members=2 -> ACTING

Interrupt the leader and watch the two modes part company. The broadcast role drops it from its membership immediately; the leader role keeps counting it, because it is LEAVING and a leader role treats that as eligible, until its heartbeat goes stale and the survivor takes the token. The status pages are on http://127.0.0.1:8081/-/cluster and :8082.

The dotenv files shorten the heartbeats so that an election and a failover happen while you watch. A real deployment leaves them alone.

examples/cluster/README.md walks through every case in detail, including what each line of output means.

docs.title: config
docs.text:
import "github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/config"

Reads a dotenv file once, then hands out typed and validated values.

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
vars, err := config.NewConfig()

NewConfig() reads the file named by INFRAPI_CONFIG_DOTENV_FILE, or .env when that variable is unset, and returns an error if the file cannot be read.

The process environment is not a fallback

Values are taken from the dotenv file only. An INFRAPI_APP_NAME exported in the shell is invisible to GetString; put it in the dotenv file, or point INFRAPI_CONFIG_DOTENV_FILE at a file that contains it.

The returned Variables exposes the raw map, the file path and the default rule set:

type Variables struct {
    Values        map[string]string
    Path          string
    DefaultConfig *DefaultConfig
}

docs.title: Reading a single value
docs.text:
Every getter takes a *VariableOpts:

type VariableOpts struct {
    Key       string // dotenv key
    Default   string // used when the key is absent or empty
    Validator string // go-playground/validator rule
    Sensible  bool   // mask the value in error messages
}

port, err := vars.GetInt(&config.VariableOpts{
    Key:       "MY_APP_PORT",
    Default:   "8080",
    Validator: "number",
})
Getter Returns Parsing GetString string raw value GetBool bool strconv.ParseBool GetInt int strconv.Atoi GetInt64 int64 strconv.ParseInt base 10 GetSliceString []string json.Unmarshal, so the value must be a JSON array GetDuration time.Duration time.ParseDuration

Rules that apply to all of them:

  • A missing or empty key with no Default is an error.
  • A missing or empty key with a Default returns that default without running the validator. Defaults are trusted.
  • Validator accepts any go-playground/validator rule string, applied to the raw string value.
  • Sensible: true replaces the value with [masked] in validation errors. Use it for tokens and passwords.
  • Every error message names the key and the dotenv path, so a bad deployment is easy to trace.

docs.title: Application configuration
docs.text:
GetAppConfig() resolves the whole INFRAPI_APP_* set in one call and returns a typed struct:

cfg, err := vars.GetAppConfig()

type AppConfig struct {
    AppName                 string
    AppLogLevel             logrus.Level
    AppLogFormat            string
    AppListenType           string
    AppListenAddress        string
    AppPlatform             string
    AppRegion               string
    AppFqdn                 string
    AppLocation             string
    AppUrl                  string
    AppTrustedProxies       []string
    AppCorsAllowOrigins     []string
    AppCorsAllowMethods     []string
    AppCorsAllowHeaders     []string
    AppCorsExposeHeaders    []string
    AppCorsAllowCredentials bool
    AppCorsMaxAge           int64
}

The first failing key aborts the call, so the error tells you exactly what to fix. Individual getters (GetAppName, GetAppLogLevel, GetAppCorsMaxAge, ...) are exported too when only one value is needed.

docs.title: Default variables
docs.text:
NewDefaultConfig() builds the rules below. A key with no default is mandatory.

Key Default Validator INFRAPI_APP_NAME - required INFRAPI_APP_LOG_LEVEL info oneof=trace debug info error INFRAPI_APP_LOG_FORMAT text oneof=text json INFRAPI_APP_LISTEN_TYPE tcp oneof=tcp systemd INFRAPI_APP_LISTEN_ADDRESS 127.0.0.1:8080 hostname_port INFRAPI_APP_FQDN os.Hostname() fqdn INFRAPI_APP_PLATFORM - oneof=sandbox preprod prod INFRAPI_APP_REGION - oneof=eu-west-1 eu-west-2 au-southeast-1 INFRAPI_APP_LOCATION - oneof=dc1 dc2 dc3 INFRAPI_APP_URL - http_url INFRAPI_APP_TRUSTED_PROXIES [] - INFRAPI_APP_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS ["*"] - INFRAPI_APP_CORS_ALLOW_METHODS ["PUT", "PATCH", "HEAD"] - INFRAPI_APP_CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS ["Origin"] - INFRAPI_APP_CORS_EXPOSE_HEADERS ["Content-Length"] - INFRAPI_APP_CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS true - INFRAPI_APP_CORS_MAX_AGE 12 -

INFRAPI_APP_CORS_MAX_AGE is a number of hours. The *_PROXIES, *_ORIGINS, *_METHODS and *_HEADERS values are JSON arrays.

docs.title: Overriding the rules
docs.text:
DefaultConfig is a plain struct of *VariableOpts, so a service can tighten or relax a rule before reading anything:

vars, err := config.NewConfig()
if err != nil {
    return err
}

vars.DefaultConfig.AppRegion.Validator = "oneof=emea apac"
vars.DefaultConfig.AppPlatform.Validator = "oneof=development staging production"

cfg, err := vars.GetAppConfig()

examples/config walks through defaults, custom validators and the error messages produced by an invalid file.

docs.title: errors
docs.text:
import infraerrors "github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/errors"

One error type for everything a service hands back to an API client. Its JSON form is an RFC 9457 problem detail, served as application/problem+json.

type Error struct {
    Type     string `json:"type,omitempty"`
    Code     int    `json:"status"`
    Title    string `json:"title"`
    Message  string `json:"detail"`
    Instance string `json:"instance,omitempty"`
    Origin   string `json:"origin,omitempty"`
    Solution string `json:"solution,omitempty"`

    Err error `json:"-"`
}
Member Meaning type URI identifying the problem type. Absent means about:blank: nothing beyond the status code. status The net/http status code. The response carries the same one. title Short summary of the problem type, identical on every occurrence. Left empty it is serialised as the status phrase, which is what about:blank requires. detail What happened this time, written for the client. instance URI identifying this occurrence: a request path, or an opaque id. origin Extension member: the failing call path, MyPackage.MyFunc.MyCall. For your operators. solution Extension member: how to fix it.

Err is the wrapped cause. It is never serialised.

docs.title: Raising an error
docs.text:
The second argument is the origin, not the title:

return infraerrors.New(http.StatusNotImplemented, "subscription.SetState",
    "state %q not supported", state)

That is a complete problem detail already: no type, so about:blank, and the title comes out as Not Implemented. Add the remediation when you know it:

return infraerrors.New(http.StatusNotFound, "user.Get", "no user with id %d", id).
    WithSolution("list the users first")

A problem clients should be able to branch on deserves a type URI, with a title describing that type rather than this occurrence:

return infraerrors.New(http.StatusConflict, "subscription.Create", "id %q is taken", id).
    WithType("https://infrapi.example.com/errors/duplicate-subscription", "Duplicate subscription")

docs.title: Wrapping a cause
docs.text:
Wrap keeps the original error reachable, so errors.Is and errors.As still work several layers up:

cfg, err := config.NewConfig()
if err != nil {
    return infraerrors.Wrap(err, http.StatusBadGateway, "config.Read", "")
}

An empty format takes the message of the cause as the detail. Pass one to say something more useful, or when the cause holds internals:

return infraerrors.Wrap(err, http.StatusBadGateway, "config.Read",
    "unable to read %s", path)

Do not flatten the cause

New(code, origin, err.Error()) compiles and reads fine, but it turns the cause into a string: every errors.Is above that point stops matching. Use Wrap.

docs.title: Finding an Error in a chain
docs.text:
As is errors.As, re-exported so a caller just checking for an *Error never needs to import the standard library errors package itself:

var apiErr *infraerrors.Error
if infraerrors.As(err, &apiErr) {
    fmt.Println(apiErr.Code, apiErr.Message)
}

Reach for the standard library's own errors.Is and errors.As directly when matching something other than *Error - a sentinel like os.ErrNotExist, or a foreign package's own error type.

The printed form carries every member that is set, which is more than the payload shows:

infrapi-error: status=502 | title=Bad Gateway | origin=config.Read | detail=unable to read app.env | cause=open app.env: no such file or directory

cause= is left out when it is already the detail.

docs.title: In a handler
docs.text:
ErrorCode picks the status of any error, whoever produced it:

Argument Result nil 0 an *Error, however deeply wrapped its Code any other error 500, since nobody identified it

ErrorCast gives the payload to serialise, synthesising an untyped 500 for a foreign error while keeping its chain:

func handle(c *gin.Context) {
    if err := doTheWork(); err != nil {
        payload, _ := json.Marshal(infraerrors.ErrorCast(err))
        c.Data(infraerrors.ErrorCode(err), infraerrors.MediaType, payload)
        return
    }
    c.JSON(http.StatusOK, result)
}

c.Data rather than c.JSON, because the payload is served as infraerrors.MediaType:

{
  "type": "https://infrapi.example.com/errors/unknown-user",
  "status": 404,
  "title": "Unknown user",
  "detail": "no user with id 42",
  "instance": "/users/42",
  "origin": "user.Get",
  "solution": "list the users first"
}

Nil in, nil out

ErrorCast(nil) returns a nil *Error. Never assign it straight to a variable of type error: a nil pointer in an error interface is not nil.

What reaches the client

Err is json:"-", so the cause is never serialised. Its text still can be: Wrap with an empty format copies err.Error() into detail, and ErrorCast does the same for a foreign error. When the cause may carry a path, a DSN or a hostname, pass an explicit format and let the real message live in your logs.

examples/errors runs all of it, payloads included.

docs.title: gateway
docs.text:
import infragateway "github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/gateway"

A client for the Apache APISIX Admin API: routes, services, upstreams and consumers as explicit CRUD methods on Client, on top of http, which supplies the TLS/mTLS, retry and timeout behaviour. Admin API failures come back as an errors.Error, so a service already handling that type elsewhere handles these too.

docs.title: Creating a client
docs.text:
client, err := infragateway.NewClient(&infragateway.ClientOptions{
    Server: "apisix-admin.example.com",
    APIKey: apiKey,
})

Server and APIKey are mandatory; everything else has a default:

Option Type Default Protocol string http Port int 9180 UserAgent string infrapi-lib-gateway GlobalTimeout int (seconds) 30 RetryCount int 3 RetryWaitTime time.Duration 1s RetryMaxWaitTime time.Duration 30s

APIKey is sent as the X-API-KEY header on every request, the authentication scheme the Admin API expects.

Update(opts) rebuilds an existing client in place with a new set of options, which is what NewClient calls internally.

client.HTTP is the *http.Client NewClient built. Every collection method sends its request through client.HTTP.NewRequest, built for exactly this - a URL that does not fit http.Client.Do's own /api/{version}/{application}/{path} shape - so this package never imports resty directly; client.HTTP's TLS, retry and timeout configuration still applies.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
Four Admin API collections are explicit methods on Client, named <Op><Type> - NewRoute, GetUpstream, ListServices, UpdateConsumer, DeleteRoute, and so on:

upstream, err := client.NewUpstream(ctx, "1", infragateway.Upstream{
    Type:  "roundrobin",
    Nodes: []infragateway.Node{{Host: "127.0.0.1", Port: 1980, Weight: 1}},
})

route, err := client.NewRoute(ctx, "1", infragateway.Route{
    URI:      "/hello",
    Upstream: upstream, // *Upstream, plugs straight in - no unwrapping
})

id, created, err := client.CreateRoute(ctx, value) // APISIX generates the id
route, err = client.GetRoute(ctx, "1")
routes, err := client.ListRoutes(ctx)
route, err = client.UpdateRoute(ctx, "1", map[string]any{"desc": "says hello"}) // partial
err = client.DeleteRoute(ctx, "1")

Routes, services and upstreams follow this pattern. Update<Type> sends a partial document - a map[string]any is the common case - and APISIX merges it into the stored value; fields left out keep their current value. New<Type> replaces the value wholesale, so use it when the caller owns the full document.

Consumers are keyed by Username rather than a generated id, so their shape is slightly different: NewConsumer(ctx, consumer) takes the id from consumer.Username instead of a separate argument, there is no CreateConsumer, and GetConsumer/UpdateConsumer/ DeleteConsumer take username where the others take id.

Every operation returns the plain domain struct - *Upstream, *Route, *Service, *Consumer - so the result of one call plugs directly into another, as Upstream does above. CreateUpstream/CreateRoute/CreateService additionally return the APISIX-generated id, since there is nowhere else to get it once you let APISIX choose.

docs.title: Health checks and timeouts
docs.text:
An Upstream carries APISIX's own health checks, timeouts and keepalive pool, typed after its schema (apisix/schema_def.lua):

upstream, err := client.NewUpstream(ctx, "api", infragateway.Upstream{
    Type:    "roundrobin",
    Nodes:   nodes,
    Timeout: &infragateway.Timeout{Connect: 2, Send: 30, Read: 120},
    Checks: &infragateway.HealthChecks{
        Active: &infragateway.ActiveCheck{
            HTTPPath:  "/readyz",
            Healthy:   &infragateway.ActiveHealthy{Interval: 2, Successes: 1},
            Unhealthy: &infragateway.ActiveUnhealthy{Interval: 1, HTTPFailures: 2},
        },
    },
})
Field APISIX member Notes Checks checks Active probes nodes on a schedule; Passive judges them by live traffic. APISIX requires Active whenever Passive is set. Timeout timeout Connect, Send and Read in seconds; APISIX requires all three. KeepalivePool keepalive_pool Size, IdleTimeout, Requests. RetryTimeout retry_timeout Seconds; 0 removes the bound.

A zero field is left out, so APISIX applies its default (each field's godoc gives it). Where APISIX gives 0 a meaning of its own - the passive counters, 0 turning that criterion off; RetryTimeout; KeepalivePool.IdleTimeout - the field is a pointer: nil leaves the default, a pointer to 0 sends 0.

Retries predates these and is a plain int: 0 is left out like any zero, so an upstream cannot ask for no retries through it.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Every error this package returns is an *errors.Error, the same RFC 9457 application error the rest of this library uses:

_, err := client.GetRoute(ctx, "1")
var apiErr *infraerrors.Error
if infraerrors.As(err, &apiErr) {
    fmt.Println(apiErr.Code, apiErr.Message)
}

// or, when only the status code matters:
code := infraerrors.ErrorCode(err)

infraerrors.As is errors.As, re-exported so this never needs the standard library errors package either - see errors.

Code is the Admin API's HTTP status for a response it sent - 404 from a Get on a deleted route, for instance, Message its error_msg when it sent one. Origin names the call that broke, in the form gateway.{collection}.{Op}, e.g. gateway.routes.Get.

A transport failure - connection refused, timeout - and a response body that fails to decode are wrapped the same way, as a 502 Bad Gateway *errors.Error carrying the underlying error as its cause, reachable with errors.Unwrap or errors.Is.

docs.title: Retry
docs.text: Retries are on by default and trigger on a transport error, 429 Too Many Requests, or any 5xx, with exponential backoff between RetryWaitTime and RetryMaxWaitTime - the same policy http applies, since that is what executes every request.

docs.title: TLS and mTLS
docs.text:
The client always negotiates TLS 1.2 or later. Certificates can be passed as PEM bytes or as filesystem paths; when both are given, the in-memory content wins.

client, err := infragateway.NewClient(&infragateway.ClientOptions{
    Server:   "apisix-admin.example.com",
    APIKey:   apiKey,
    Protocol: "https",

    CACertPath: "/etc/ssl/certs/internal-ca.pem",

    ClientCertPath: "/etc/ssl/certs/myapp.pem",
    ClientKeyPath:  "/etc/ssl/private/myapp.key",
})
Option Purpose CACertContent / CACertPath Trust an internal CA for the server certificate. ClientCertContent / ClientKeyContent mTLS keypair from memory. ClientCertPath / ClientKeyPath mTLS keypair from disk.

An mTLS keypair needs both halves: cert and key must come from the same source.

docs.title: Escape hatch
docs.text:
client.HTTP.RestyClient is the underlying *resty.Client. Anything neither wrapper exposes - middlewares, proxies, custom transports - is configurable there.

examples/gateway runs all of this against a local stand-in for the Admin API, including the error paths above.

docs.title: Testing against a real APISIX
docs.text:
pkg/gateway's own tests run against a local stand-in for the Admin API, same as the example - no real APISIX required. TestIntegration_RealAdminAPI is the exception: it drives a real, already-running Admin API through an upstream, a service, a route and a consumer, and is the test to run while building or verifying your own integration. It is skipped unless APISIX_ADMIN_SERVER and APISIX_ADMIN_APIKEY are set:

APISIX_ADMIN_SERVER=127.0.0.1 APISIX_ADMIN_APIKEY=<your-admin-key> \
    go test ./pkg/gateway/... -run TestIntegration_RealAdminAPI -v

APISIX_ADMIN_PROTOCOL and APISIX_ADMIN_PORT override the http/9180 defaults. The test cleans up everything it creates, whether it passes or fails.

docs.title: http
docs.text:
import infrahttp "github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/http"

A resty client with InfraPI defaults: bearer token, JSON headers, TLS 1.2 floor, retry on transient failures and optional hedging.

docs.title: Creating a client
docs.text:
client, err := infrahttp.NewClient(&infrahttp.ClientOptions{
    Server:      "api.example.com",
    Application: "myapp",
    Token:       token,
})

Server and Application are mandatory; everything else has a default:

Option Type Default Protocol string https Port int 443 APIVersion string v1 UserAgent string infrapi-lib-http-{application} Headers map[string]string Content-Type and Accept set to application/json GlobalTimeout int (seconds) 60 RetryCount int 3 RetryWaitTime time.Duration 1s RetryMaxWaitTime time.Duration 30s

Token, when set, is sent as a bearer token on every request.

Update(opts) rebuilds an existing client in place with a new set of options, which is what NewClient calls internally.

docs.title: Request URL
docs.text:
Paths are relative. The client builds:

{Protocol}://{Server}:{Port}/api/{APIVersion}/{Application}/{path}

So client.Get("status", nil) on the client above requests https://api.example.com:443/api/v1/myapp/status.

docs.title: Sending requests
docs.text:
resp, err := client.Post("items", &infrahttp.RequestOptions{
    Data:    body,                                   // raw request body
    Headers: map[string]string{"X-Request-Id": id},  // merged into the request
    Server:  "api-eu.example.com",                   // per-request host override
})

Get, Post, Put, Patch, Delete and Head all delegate to Do(method, path, opts), and opts may be nil.

type Response struct {
    Code int
    Body []byte
}

Response is always returned, even alongside an error, so the status code and body of a failed call stay readable. When the transport itself fails, Code is 500.

docs.title: Success range
docs.text:
A response is an error when its status code is below MinHttpCode or above MaxHttpCode. The defaults are 200 and 400, and both bounds are inclusive, so a 400 Bad Request counts as success unless the range is narrowed:

resp, err := client.Get("status", &infrahttp.RequestOptions{
    MinHttpCode: 200,
    MaxHttpCode: 299,
})

The error message is the HTTP status text; inspect resp.Body for the server payload.

docs.title: Retry
docs.text:
Retries are on by default and trigger on a transport error, 429 Too Many Requests, or any 5xx, with exponential backoff between RetryWaitTime and RetryMaxWaitTime.

client, err := infrahttp.NewClient(&infrahttp.ClientOptions{
    Server:           "api.example.com",
    Application:      "myapp",
    RetryCount:       5,
    RetryWaitTime:    200 * time.Millisecond,
    RetryMaxWaitTime: 5 * time.Second,
})

docs.title: Hedging
docs.text:
Hedging fires staggered concurrent requests and keeps the first success, trading extra load for a shorter tail latency.

client, err := infrahttp.NewClient(&infrahttp.ClientOptions{
    Server:      "api.example.com",
    Application: "myapp",
    Hedging: &infrahttp.HedgingOptions{
        Enabled:      true,
        Delay:        150 * time.Millisecond,
        UpTo:         2,
        MaxPerSecond: 5,
    },
})
Field Meaning Enabled Turns hedging on. Delay Wait before each additional request. 0 sends them immediately. UpTo Maximum concurrent hedged requests. Anything below 2 leaves hedging inert. MaxPerSecond Rate cap across hedged requests, fractional allowed. 0 is unlimited. NonReadOnlyAllowed Also hedge POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE.

Warning

Hedging duplicates requests. It is limited to GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE unless NonReadOnlyAllowed is set, and resty disables retry while hedging is on.

docs.title: TLS and mTLS
docs.text:
The client always negotiates TLS 1.2 or later. Certificates can be passed as PEM bytes or as filesystem paths; when both are given, the in-memory content wins.

client, err := infrahttp.NewClient(&infrahttp.ClientOptions{
    Server:      "api.example.com",
    Application: "myapp",

    CACertPath: "/etc/ssl/certs/internal-ca.pem",

    ClientCertPath: "/etc/ssl/certs/myapp.pem",
    ClientKeyPath:  "/etc/ssl/private/myapp.key",
})
Option Purpose CACertContent / CACertPath Trust an internal CA for the server certificate. ClientCertContent / ClientKeyContent mTLS keypair from memory. ClientCertPath / ClientKeyPath mTLS keypair from disk.

An mTLS keypair needs both halves: cert and key must come from the same source.

docs.title: A different URL shape
docs.text:
Do always builds {Protocol}://{Server}:{Port}/api/{APIVersion}/{Application}/{path}. A caller targeting something else - a third-party API with its own path layout - uses NewRequest instead, which keeps this client's TLS, retry, header and timeout configuration without going through that URL template, and without exposing resty to the caller:

resp, err := client.NewRequest(ctx).
    SetBody(payload).
    Post("https://third-party.example.com/v2/widgets")

NewRequest(ctx) returns a *Request with Get, Post, Put, Patch and Delete, each taking the full URL and returning the same *Response as Do. Unlike Do, a Request applies no success-range check: any response that comes back, 2xx or not, is returned without an error, and the caller decides what counts as a failure. pkg/gateway is built this way, on top of NewRequest rather than resty directly.

StatusText(code) and the StatusBadGateway constant are net/http's own, re-exported so a caller deciding what counts as a failure - and building an errors.Error to report it - never needs to import net/http itself either:

if resp.Code < 200 || resp.Code >= 300 {
    return infraerrors.New(resp.Code, "myapp.Call", "%s", infrahttp.StatusText(resp.Code))
}

docs.title: Escape hatch
docs.text:
client.RestyClient is the underlying *resty.Client. Anything neither wrapper exposes - middlewares, cookies, proxies, custom transports - is configurable there.

examples/http runs all of this against a local server, including retry and hedging.

docs.title: listener
docs.text:
import "github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/listener"

Opens the socket a service accepts connections on, from the same AppConfig the server package consumes.

ln, err := listener.Listen(cfg)
if err != nil {
    return err
}

cfg.AppListenType decides what happens:

Type Behaviour tcp Binds cfg.AppListenAddress, the default 127.0.0.1:8080. systemd Adopts the socket systemd passed through socket activation. anything else Error. The dotenv validator already rejects it at load time.

docs.title: With the server package
docs.text:
Listen returns a plain net.Listener and NewServerGin returns a plain http.Handler, so the two meet at http.Server:

ln, err := listener.Listen(cfg)
if err != nil {
    return err
}

engine, err := server.NewServerGin(cfg)
if err != nil {
    return err
}

srv := &http.Server{Handler: engine, ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second}
if err := srv.Serve(ln); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
    return err
}

Nothing about the service changes between a TCP socket and an activated one: the same binary serves whichever Listen returns.

docs.title: Socket activation
docs.text:
Under systemd the socket is opened by the unit and handed to the process on file descriptor 3, announced through two environment variables:

  • LISTEN_PID must equal the PID of the process, otherwise the descriptor belongs to someone else and Listen refuses it.
  • LISTEN_FDS is the number of descriptors passed; 0 means systemd has a problem, and only the first descriptor is used.

The descriptor is adopted with net.FileListener, which duplicates it, so the one systemd passed is closed once the listener exists. No systemd library is pulled in for this.

A matching unit pair looks like:

myservice.socket
[Socket]
ListenStream=127.0.0.1:8080

[Install]
WantedBy=sockets.target
myservice.service
[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/bin/myservice
Environment=INFRAPI_APP_LISTEN_TYPE=systemd

examples/listener runs the TCP path, serves the gin engine on it, and shows both error paths.

docs.title: server
docs.text:
import "github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/server"

One constructor that turns an *config.AppConfig into a ready *gin.Engine.

engine, err := server.NewServerGin(cfg)
if err != nil {
    return err
}

if err := engine.Run(cfg.AppListenAddress); err != nil {
    return err
}

docs.title: What it wires
docs.text:
• Trusted proxies from AppTrustedProxies. An invalid entry is returned as an error instead of being ignored, so a bad INFRAPI_APP_TRUSTED_PROXIES fails at startup.
  • CORS from the AppCors* fields. AppCorsMaxAge is read as hours.
  • Recovery and access logging, written to gin.DefaultWriter. Their format follows AppLogFormat (INFRAPI_APP_LOG_FORMAT): gin's text lines by default, or with json one JSON object per line, as below.
  • Request metrics, recorded for every route.
  • Four endpoints, with nothing to configure:
Endpoint Serves GET /-/metadata The application identity. GET /-/metrics Prometheus exposition format. GET /-/openapi.json OpenAPI 3.1, generated from the route table - unless the service passes its own documents with WithOpenAPI. GET /-/docs Swagger UI reading that specification, or the documents passed with WithOpenAPI.

The paths are exported as server.MetricsPath, server.OpenAPIPath and server.DocsPath.

/-/metadata answers with:

{
  "appName": "my-service",
  "appPlatform": "sandbox",
  "appRegion": "eu-west-1",
  "appLocation": "dc1",
  "appFqdn": "my-service.example.com",
  "appUrl": "http://my-service.example.com:8080"
}

Nothing else is registered. The engine is a normal *gin.Engine: add groups, routes and middleware on top of it.

v1 := engine.Group("/api/v1")
v1.GET("/widgets", listWidgets)

docs.title: Your own OpenAPI documents
docs.text:
The generated specification knows paths and parameters, not bodies or schemas. A service whose contract is written by hand passes it with WithOpenAPI, and /-/docs documents that instead:

//go:embed api/orders/v1.yaml
var ordersV1 []byte

engine, err := server.NewServerGin(cfg, server.WithOpenAPI(
    server.OpenAPISpec{Name: "orders v1", Path: "orders/v1.yaml", Content: ordersV1},
))
  • Each document is served as it is under server.OpenAPIPrefix, here /-/openapi/orders/v1.yaml, as application/yaml (.yaml, .yml) or application/json (.json).
  • With several documents — one file per major version, say — Swagger UI offers them in a selector.
  • They replace the generated specification: /-/openapi.json is no longer served, so the API has one description, not two.
  • NewServerGin refuses a document without a name or content, a path that is absolute, not clean or not .json/.yaml/.yml, and two documents sharing a name or a path.

With INFRAPI_APP_LOG_FORMAT=json, every request is one line:

{"time":"2026-10-05T10:12:03.481Z","level":"info","msg":"request","method":"GET","path":"/users/42","route":"/users/:id","status":200,"latency_ms":1.204,"client_ip":"10.0.0.7","size":118,"user_agent":"curl/8.11.1","request_id":"5f0c…"}
  • time, level and msg are the names logrus's JSONFormatter uses, so a service that logs through logrus with that formatter writes lines a collector parses the same way. level is warning for a 4xx and error for a 5xx.
  • path is the URL path without its query string; route is the route pattern, empty when no route matched.
  • request_id is X-Request-Id, from the request or else from the response.
  • errors carries what handlers attached with c.Error, when they did.

A recovered panic is one line too, its stack in a field, followed by the line of the request it ended with a 500:

{"time":"…","level":"error","msg":"panic recovered","method":"GET","path":"/boom","panic":"kaboom","stack":"/src/handler.go:42 (0x4f2a1c)\n\t(*Handler).Get: return h.store.Get(id)\n…"}

The recovery is gin's, with JSON lines:

  • The stack has gin's text format and starts where the panic was raised: one file:line (0xpc) line and one <tab>function: source line line per frame. The source line is ??? when the file is not there, as in an image that ships only the binary; gin drops the function line in that case, this keeps it.
  • A client that closed the connection (EPIPE, ECONNRESET, http.ErrAbortHandler) is not a panic: one warning line, "msg":"client connection broken" with the error, no stack, and nothing written back to a connection that is gone.
  • gin's text recovery dumps the request in debug mode, every header but Authorization — an apikey header included. The JSON lines never do.

docs.title: Fields of your own
docs.text:
server.LogField adds a member to the line of the current request — what the service knows and the engine cannot:

// in a gin handler
server.LogField(c, "tenant", tenant)

// in a net/http handler mounted with gin.WrapH, or its middleware
server.LogField(r.Context(), "resource", map[string]string{"kind": "folder", "id": id})

{"time":"…","level":"info","msg":"request","method":"POST",…,"resource":{"id":"f1","kind":"folder"},"tenant":"acme"}

Your fields come after the engine's, in key order. The value is marshalled to JSON (one that cannot be is written as its %v text); setting a key again replaces it. The engine's own names (time, level, msg, method, path, route, status, latency_ms, client_ip, size, user_agent, request_id, errors, error, panic, stack) are refused, so nothing can hide what the engine saw. With text logs LogField does nothing.

The engine leaves the global logrus logger alone: a service that wants its own lines in JSON sets logrus.SetFormatter(&logrus.JSONFormatter{}) itself.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Two collectors are recorded for every request, carrying the service FQDN in a name label:

http_requests_total{method="GET",name="my-service.example.com",path="/api/v1/widgets/:id",status="200"} 1
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{method="GET",name="my-service.example.com",path="/api/v1/widgets/:id",le="0.005"} 1

path is the route pattern, not the URL, so /widgets/1 and /widgets/2 share one time series. A request that matched no route is labelled unmatched, which keeps a scan or a 404 flood from creating a series per URL.

The endpoint also gathers the default registry, so anything the service registers itself, with promauto or otherwise, is exposed alongside the Go runtime collectors:

var widgets = promauto.NewCounter(prometheus.CounterOpts{
    Name: "widgets_created_total",
    Help: "Widgets created.",
})

docs.title: OpenAPI
docs.text:
The specification is generated per request from engine.Routes(), so routes added after NewServerGin are in it. Gin path parameters become OpenAPI ones: /widgets/:id is served as /widgets/{id} with a required string path parameter, and /files/*filepath the same way.

info.title is AppName, info.version is the version of the binary as reported by runtime/debug, and servers holds AppUrl.

What the route table cannot tell

Gin knows methods, paths and path parameters. It does not know request bodies, query parameters, response schemas or status codes, so the document does not invent them: every operation carries a single default response marked as undocumented. It is an accurate map of the surface, not a contract.

The docs page loads Swagger UI from a CDN

/-/docs is a small HTML page pulling a pinned Swagger UI release from cdn.jsdelivr.net. A browser without internet access renders an empty page, while the documents themselves - /-/openapi.json, or those under /-/openapi/ - keep working: they are served in process and depend on nothing external.

docs.title: Configuration in memory
docs.text:
AppConfig is a plain struct, so settings can be adjusted before the engine is built - useful for tests and for values that are not worth a dotenv key:

cfg.AppCorsAllowOrigins = []string{"https://app.example.com"}
cfg.AppTrustedProxies = []string{"10.0.0.0/8"}

engine, err := server.NewServerGin(cfg)

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
NewServerGin returns the handler, not a running server, so the lifecycle stays in your hands. Pair it with listener when the socket comes from the configuration or from systemd:

srv := &http.Server{
    Addr:              cfg.AppListenAddress,
    Handler:           engine,
    ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
}

go func() {
    if err := srv.ListenAndServe(); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}()

quit := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
signal.Notify(quit, syscall.SIGINT, syscall.SIGTERM)
<-quit

ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
defer cancel()
if err := srv.Shutdown(ctx); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

examples/server runs this end to end, including a live request against /-/metadata.

docs.title: tofu
docs.text:
import "github.com/infrapi/lib/pkg/tofu"

Drives OpenTofu-protocol provider plugins — terraform-provider-local, any provider from the registry, or a custom one — for any resource type, using github.com/opentofu/provider-client as its transport, and layers a declarative, data-described apply/destroy on top.

provider-client models the wire protocol closely: a caller builds requests and decodes responses as cty.Value against a schema it fetched itself, and reproduces the small slice of OpenTofu core business logic (proposed new state, destroy plans, ...) needed to drive a resource through create, read, update and delete. This package does that once, generically, so callers describe resources with plain map[string]any configuration instead:

provider, err := tofu.Start(ctx, "local", "./terraform-provider-local")
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer provider.Close()

if err := provider.Configure(ctx, "1.15.5", nil); err != nil {
    return err
}

res, err := provider.Create(ctx, "local_file", map[string]any{
    "content":  "foo!",
    "filename": "./foo.bar",
})

res is a Resource: its attributes as a plain Go map, plus the bookkeeping data the provider needs to see again in Read, Update or Delete. Persisting it between runs is the caller's job; this package keeps none of its own state.

docs.title: Multiple providers
docs.text:
A Registry keeps a set of named, running providers, so a caller can drive resources across several plugins at once and close every one of them together:

registry := tofu.NewRegistry()
defer registry.Close()

local, err := registry.Start(ctx, "local", "./terraform-provider-local")
random, err := registry.Start(ctx, "random", "./terraform-provider-random")

docs.title: Declarative apply
docs.text:
A Plan lists the provider plugins to launch and the resources each one owns, as data:

plan := tofu.Plan{
    Providers: []tofu.ProviderSpec{
        {Name: "local", Executable: "./terraform-provider-local"},
    },
    Resources: []tofu.ResourceSpec{
        {
            Provider: "local", Address: "local_file.foo", ResourceType: "local_file",
            Config: map[string]any{"content": "foo!", "filename": "./foo.bar"},
        },
    },
}

result, err := tofu.Apply(ctx, plan, nil)

Apply starts every provider the plan names, applies every resource in declaration order — creating an address absent from prior, updating one present in it — and closes every provider before returning. Destroy does the same in reverse, deleting instead of creating or updating:

if err := tofu.Destroy(ctx, plan, result.Resources); err != nil {
    return err
}

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This package stops at single-resource operations and a thin declarative layer on top of them:

  • No state persistence. A Resource is a snapshot, and Result.Resources from Apply is how a caller carries state between runs; saving and loading it is up to the caller.
  • No dependency graph across resources. Plan.Resources is processed in the order it is listed (reverse order for Destroy); order it so anything a resource's config depends on comes earlier in the slice.
  • No plan preview or approval step: Apply and Destroy both act immediately.
  • Update cannot detect that a provider requires replacement (destroy then re-create) for a given attribute change, because the underlying provider-client library does not currently expose that information. A provider that needs replacement typically returns incomplete state for an in-place update, which this package reports as an error rather than returning silently-wrong data; call Delete then Create instead for a resource type known to require replacement for the attributes being changed.

examples/tofu applies a plan with two resources, re-applies it to show the second run updates in place, then destroys it.
